Paul quotes David using covered to refer to God forgiving sins as if he covers sins so that he no longer sees them.

11:17: Paul continues using the metaphor of a tree to speak about how God rejected unbelieving Jews and accepted non-Jews to be part of his people instead. The olive tree represents God’s people. The branches that were broken off represent Jews who do not believe in Jesus. The wild olive branch represents non-Jewish people who believe in Jesus. The richness represents the blessings God gives his people. The root represents either the ancestors of the Israelites (as in the previous verse) or the Jewish people in general. See also the discussion of this metaphor in the introduction for this chapter.
Even though Paul is writing to a group of people, non-Jewish Christians, you is singular throughout this verse.
11:18: Paul continues using the metaphor of a tree from the previous two verses. Here, branches represents those Jews whom God rejected because they did not believe in Jesus. The root represents either the ancestors of the Israelites (like in 11:16) or the Jewish people in general. See also the discussion of this metaphor in the introduction for this chapter.
Paul implies that Gentile believers who boast should remember that they are supported by the root of the faith of Abraham and the first Israelites.
11:20: This sentence introduces Paul’s response to the statement in the previous verse.
Paul speaks of Gentile believers remaining part of God’s people as if they were standing firm.
The phrase in faith could indicate: (1) the means by which Gentile believers should stand firm; (2) the reason why Gentile believers should stand firm.

Here, arrogant things refers to the arrogant thoughts that a Gentile Christian might have against the Jews. Specifically, they might think that they are better than Jews who are not Christian, as indicated by the previous verse.
11:21: Here, natural branches refers to the Jewish people who rejected Jesus.
Paul implies that God will not spare anyone who stops trusting in Jesus.
11:22: Paul uses the term See to focus his audiences’ attention on what he is about to say.
Here Paul speaks of God’s severity as if it were an object that could be on someone. He means that God punishes them severely.
Paul refers to the Jews who failed to trust God as if they were people who fell.
Here Paul speaks of God’s kindness as if it were an object that could be on someone. He means that God acts kindly toward those who trust in Jesus.
Here Paul speaks of God’s kindness as if it were a place in which someone could continue staying. He means that his readers should continue trusting in God’s kindness.
Here Paul refers to his Gentile Christian audience as if they were branches that God could cut off. He means that God would reject them if they do not remain faithful.
11:23: Paul speaks of the Jews becoming part of God’s people as if they were branches that could be grafted in to a tree.
11:24: Paul continues speaking of the Gentile believers and Jews as if they were branches of a tree, as he did in 11:17–22. Here, a wild olive tree represents all non-Jewish people who do not believe in Jesus, cut off represents being separated from unbelieving non-Jewish people, and good olive tree and their own olive tree represents God’s people.
Paul is not asking for information, but is using the question form here to emphasize the truth of what he is saying.
11:25: Paul uses the word mystery to refer to God saving a remnant of Jews after he saves a certain amount of Gentiles. This does not mean that the idea is hard to understand, but rather, God had not yet revealed it to people.
Here, wise in yourselves refers to someone arrogantly thinking that he is wiser than he really is.
Here, hardening refers to being stubborn and unwilling to believe in Jesus. This hardening is only partial because some Jews believe in Jesus.
Here, fullness refers to the full amount of non-Jewish people whom God will save.
Here Paul uses come in to speak about people joining God’s people as if they were entering a place.
11:26: Here, thus indicates that all Israel will be saved in the same manner as “the fullness of the Gentiles,” as mentioned in the previous verse.
Paul quotes Isaiah speaking of ungodly things as if they were an object that someone could turn away.
Here, Jacob refers to the descendants of Jacob, who are also called Israelites.
11:27: Paul quotes God speaking of sins as if they were objects that someone could take away. He means that people are forgiven for the sins they have done.
11:28: Here Paul implies that the Jewish people are rejecting the gospel.
Paul implies that the Jewish people are enemies of God because they rejected the gospel.
Here, for the sake of their forefathers refers to the promises that God made to their forefathers.
11:31: Here, your mercy refers to the mercy that God has shown to non-Jewish people whom he saves.
11:32: συνέκλεισεν … ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς πάντας εἰς ἀπείθειαν
Here Paul refers to people whom God allows to disobey him as if they were prisoners shut up in a prison.
11:33: βάθος πλούτου, καὶ σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως Θεοῦ
Here Paul refers to God’s wealth, wisdom, and knowledge as if they were like a deep place. He means that God’s wealth, wisdom, and knowledge are truly great.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Paul uses them to emphasize what he is saying.
Here Paul speaks of God’s judgments as if they were objects that people cannot search for. He means that people cannot fully understand God’s judgments.
Here Paul speaks of God’s ways as if they were objects that people cannot discover. He means that people cannot fully understand God’s ways.
11:34: Paul quotes Isaiah using this question to emphasize that no one is as wise as the Lord.
Here, mind refers to what a person knows and thinks.
11:35: τίς προέδωκεν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἀνταποδοθήσεται αὐτῷ
Paul quotes Job using this question to emphasize what he is saying.
11:36: Here, from indicates that all things came from God because he made them.
Here, through indicates that God is the means by which all things continue to exist.
Here, to indicates that God is the reason all things exist.
12:1: παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν

Here Paul refers to a believer in Christ who obeys God as if that person were one of the animals that the Jews killed and then offered to God as a sacrifice, except that this sacrifice is still living.
12:2: Here, this age refers to the attitudes and actions of the unbelievers who live during this period of time.
Here Paul speaks of changing the way a person thinks as if that person’s mind is being renewed.
12:3: διὰ τῆς χάριτος τῆς δοθείσης μοι
Here, grace refers to God graciously choosing Paul to be an apostle.
μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ’ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν
Here, think more highly of himself refers to someone arrogantly thinking that he is better than he really is.
ἑκάστῳ ὡς ὁ Θεὸς ἐμέρισεν μέτρον πίστεως
Here, faith could refer to: (1) different degrees of faith in God that God gives believers; (2) the spiritual gifts that result from faith and are given to believers in different degrees.
12:4: Here, just as indicates that what follows in this verse is a simile. Paul uses this simile to compare all believers in Christ to the parts of a human body.
12:5: τὸ δὲ καθ’ εἷς ἀλλήλων μέλη
Paul speaks of the believers as if God had physically joined them together like the parts of the human body are joined.
12:6: Paul speaks of the different abilities to serve other believers that God gives believers as being gracious gifts from God.
Here Paul uses faith in the same way he did in 12:3.
12:11: Here, the spirit could refer to: (1) a person’s spirit, as in 1:9; (2) the Holy Spirit.
12:12: Here, in indicates that prayer is what one needs to do persistently.
12:13: Here Paul implies sharing the things that a person has with those saints who have needs.
12:14: These two commands mean the same thing. Paul uses them to emphasize what he is saying.
12:16: This clause is an idiom that refers to having the same concern for the wellbeing of other people as a person has for himself.
Here, thinking the high things refers to someone arrogantly thinking that he is better than other people.
Here, the lowly ones could refer to: (1) people who are poor or are not respected by society; (2) doings things that people think are humiliating or unimportant.
12:17: Here Paul uses paying back to refer to doing something evil to someone in response to the evil that person has done.
Here Paul uses sight to refer to what people mentally perceive.
12:19: These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize that God will avenge his people.
Here Moses quotes God using repay to refer to appropriately punishing someone as if the punishment were reciprocal payment for that person’s deeds.
12:20: ἄνθρακας πυρὸς σωρεύσεις ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ

This clause is an idiom. It could refer to: (1) a person feeling shame as a result of being helped by someone whom that person had harmed; (2) God very severely punishing the person who is being helped.
12:21: Paul describes evil as if it were a person who could conquer someone or be conquered by someone. He is referring to someone doing evil in response to someone doing evil to that person.
13:1: Paul uses soul here to refer to the whole life of a person.
13:2: Here Paul speaks of judgment as if it were an object that one could bring and put on someone.
13:3: Here, the good deed and the evil deed refer to the people who do those deeds.
θέλεις δὲ μὴ φοβεῖσθαι τὴν ἐξουσίαν
Paul is not asking for information, but is using the question form here to emphasize the truth of what he is saying.
13:4: Here Paul uses a figure of speech that expresses a strong positive meaning by using a negative word together with a word that means the opposite of the intended meaning.
Here, the sword refers to a ruler’s authority to punish wicked people, which could include killing them with a sword.
Paul speaks of wrath as if it were an object that could be put on a person. He means that every evil person will experience wrathful punishment.
13:5: Paul implies that his readers should be subjected to the rulers described in 13:1–4.
13:6: Here, this very thing refers to serving God by ruling over people, as is indicated by Paul calling them servants of God in the previous clause.
13:7: The word toll refers to a specific kind of tax that must be paid in addition to regular taxes.
Here Paul refers to fearing and honoring those who deserve to be feared and honored as if someone is paying them fear and honor.
13:8: μηδενὶ μηδὲν ὀφείλετε, εἰ μὴ τὸ ἀλλήλους ἀγαπᾶν
Here Paul speaks of loving other believers as if it were a debt owed to them.
Here, one another refers to other Christians.
13:9: Here, any other commandment refers to any of the commandments that God gave the Israelites other than those that Paul has just mentioned.
Here Paul uses word to refer to a commandment that is made up of words.
13:10: ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται
Here Paul speaks of love as if it were a person who could do some kind of work. He means that people who love other people do not do evil things to them.
13:11: Paul is leaving out a word that a sentence would need in many languages to be complete.
Here, hour refers to a point in time when something happens. It has the same meaning as time in the previous clause. It does not refer to a 60-minute length of time.
Paul speaks of the need for the Roman believers to be spiritually vigilant as if they needed to wake up from being asleep.
Here Paul uses salvation to refer to the future event when Christ returns and Christians receive the full blessings of their salvation.
Here Paul speaks of our salvation as if it were an object that could become nearer to a person. He means that our salvation will occur soon.
This phrase indicates the time at which Paul’s Christian readers first started believing in Jesus.
13:12: The night here refers the time period when people do evil deeds.
Here, advanced refers to the night being almost over.

Paul speaks of the time when Jesus will return to earth as the day. This event is referred to as “the day of the Lord” elsewhere in the Bible and is related to Paul’s reference to a future “salvation” in the previous verse.
Here Paul speaks of the day as if it were an object that could come near a person. He means that the time when Jesus returns will be soon.
ἀποθώμεθα οὖν τὰ ἔργα τοῦ σκότους
Here, put off means to completely stop doing something, and the works of the darkness refers to evil deeds.
Here, put on means to start doing something.
Here, weapons refers to what Christians do to oppose evil, and the light refers to good deeds, which is in contrast to the darkness in the previous clause.
13:13: Here Paul uses walk to refer to how people behave or lives their lives.
Here Paul refers to the unashamed way that Christians are supposed to behave as if they were walking during the day, when people can see what they do.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize all kinds of sexual sins.
13:14: Paul speaks of Christ as if he were clothing that someone could put on. He means that people should behave like Jesus behaves.
Here Paul uses flesh figuratively to refer to sinful human nature.
14:1: Here, weak in the faith refers to someone who does not have a mature faith, but feels guilty about doing certain things that God did not forbid. The word weak here does not refer to physical weakness. See the discussion of this in the introduction for this chapter.
14:2: Here Paul implies that this person eats only vegetables.
14:3: Here, the one eating refers to the person mentioned in the previous verse who believes that he can eat any kind of food, and the one not eating refers to the person called “the one being weak” in the previous two verses.
14:4: σὺ τίς εἶ, ὁ κρίνων ἀλλότριον οἰκέτην
Paul is using a question to emphasize that Christians should not judge each other.
Even though Paul is writing to a group of people, you here is singular.
Paul speaks of any Christian as if he were a household slave who belongs to another. He means that all Christians belong to God.
Paul speaks of God as if he were a master who owns slaves.

This could mean: (1) stands and stand refer to pleasing God, and falls refers to not pleasing God; (2) stands and stand refer to being accepted by God at the final judgment, and falls refers to being condemned by God at the final judgment.
14:5: ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ, πληροφορείσθω
Paul implies that each person should be convinced about what he thinks honors the Lord.
14:6: The one regarding refers to the person in the previous verse who “judges day from day”.
Here Paul speaks of expressing thanks as if words of gratitude were something that could be given to a person.
14:7: Here, for himself means to do something only to benefit oneself.
14:8: Here, for the Lord means to do something only to benefit the Lord.
14:10: Even though Paul is writing to a group of people, you and your here are singular.
Paul is using two questions here to emphasize that Christians should not judge each other.
πάντες … παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι τοῦ Θεοῦ

Here, present ourselves before refers to standing in front of a judge in order to be judged, and the judgment seat of God refers to the place where God judges. Paul means that all believers will be judged by God.
14:11: This phrase is used to start an oath or solemn promise.
Paul uses the words knee and tongue to refer to the entire person who is doing these acts.
This action was an expression of worship in this culture.
14:13: τὸ μὴ τιθέναι πρόσκομμα τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἢ σκάνδαλον
Here, stumbling block and trap mean basically the same thing. They both refer to tempting someone to sin. Paul uses them to emphasize what he is saying.
14:14: οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ
Here, know and am persuaded mean very similar things. Paul uses them to emphasize what he is saying.
Here, in could indicate: (1) the means by which Paul was persuaded; (2) Paul being united with Christ.
The next verse indicates that here Paul is specifically referring to unclean foods, which were foods that Jews were forbidden to eat according to the law of Moses.
14:15: This phrase refers to a Christian eating food that another Christians thinks is unclean, as mentioned in the previous verse and 14:2–6.
Even though Paul is writing to a group of people, your and you here are singular.
Here, hurt refers to experiencing emotional or spiritual offense or suffering. It does not refer to being physically injured.
Here Paul uses walking to refer to how people behave or live their lives. See similar uses of “walk” in 6:4, 8:4, and 13:13.
Paul uses destroy here to refer to causing someone to stop trusting in Jesus, which will result in that person experiencing punishment forever in hell.
This phrase refers to a Christian eating food that another Christian thinks is unclean, as mentioned in the previous verse and 14:2–6.
14:16: Here, good could refer to: (1) the good things that God gives Christians; (2) the freedom that Christians have to eat any food they want to eat.
14:17: Here, is not indicates that what follows is what the kingdom of God does not consist of or is not concerned with.
Here, in the Holy Spirit could refer to: (1) the means by which Christians experience righteousness and peace and joy; (2) Christians being united with the Holy Spirit.
14:18: Here, this way refers to the “righteousness and peace and joy” mentioned in the previous verse.
14:19: Here Paul refers to the things of peace and the things of the building up as if they were something that people could pursue. He is telling Christians to do these things.
τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς τῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους
Here, Paul speaks of helping other Christians become more spiritually mature as if one were building up a building.
14:20: μὴ … κατάλυε τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ
Here, tear down refers to undoing the work God has done.
This phrase refers to a Christian eating food that another Christian thinks is unclean, as mentioned in 14:2–6, 13–17.
Here, things refers to food and clean refers to something that God has permitted.
τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ διὰ προσκόμματος ἐσθίοντι
Here, eats with a stumbling block refers to tempting another believer to sin by eating food that the other believer thinks is sinful to eat.
14:21: Even though Paul is writing to a group of people, your here is singular.
Here, stumbles refers to another believer succumbing to the temptation to sin.

Here, weak refers to being spiritually immature.
14:22: Here, faith refers to what Christians believe that God permits them to do, as mentioned in 14:1–6.
Even though Paul is writing to a group of people, you and yourself here are singular.
κατὰ σεαυτὸν ἔχε ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ
This clause refers to keeping one’s beliefs between oneself and God, rather than telling other people about them.

Here Paul speaks of people keeping what they believe before God as if they were standing in front of God. Paul means that people should keep private their beliefs about what God permits them to do, as if God is the only one who knows about those beliefs.
Here, judge refers to feeling guilty or condemning oneself.
14:23: This phrase refers to a person who has determined that eating certain foods is prohibited by God.
Paul implies that the person eats what that person believes God has forbidden to be eaten.
In this verse from refers to what a person bases their actions on.
Here, all refers to anything that a person does.
15:1: Here, we, being able refers to Paul and other people who have mature faith. See the discussion about this in the introduction for this chapter.
Paul speaks of weaknesses as if they were objects that a person could bear. He means that mature Christians should patiently help spiritually weak Christians.
Here, the ones who are unable refers to Christians who are not spiritually mature. See the discussion of this in the introduction for this chapter.

οἱ ὀνειδισμοὶ τῶν ὀνειδιζόντων σε, ἐπέπεσαν ἐπ’ ἐμέ
Paul quotes David referring to insults against God also affecting Christ as if those insults were objects that fell on him.
15:4: Paul is referring to what was previously written in the Scriptures.
Here Paul speaks about the Scriptures as if they were a person who could have patience and be encouraging. He means that God uses the Scriptures to show his patience and encouragement.
15:5: This could refer to: (1) the example of Christ; (2) the will of Christ; (3) both the example and will of Christ.
15:6: Here, glorify with one mouth refers to being united while praising God aloud.
15:8: Here, the circumcision refers to the people who have been circumcised: the Jews.
15:10: Here, again indicates that what follows is another quotation from Scripture that expresses the same idea of the quotation in the previous verse.
15:12: These three expressions all refer to the same person, the Messiah.
Paul quotes Isaiah referring to a descendant of Jesse as if that person were a root or shoot that had grown out of a plant.
Paul quotes Isaiah using rising to refer to someone becoming a king.
15:13: Paul refers to people experiencing joy and peace as if they were things that could fill someone.
Here, in indicates that believing is the means by which people will experience all joy and peace.
15:14: Paul uses the words myself and yourselves to emphasize how certain he is that his readers are good and knowledgeable Christians.
Paul refers to people experiencing goodness as if it were something that could make someone full.
Here Paul refers to people having knowledge as if it were something that someone could be filled with.
Here, all is an exaggeration that Paul uses to emphasize how much knowledge these people have.
15:15: Here, in part refers to some parts of this letter.
Here, grace refers to God graciously choosing Paul to be an apostle.
15:16: Paul speaks of his preaching the gospel to the Gentiles as if he is a priest who serves the gospel by making an offering to God. He speaks of the Gentiles who become Christians as a result of his preaching as if they were the offering that he makes.
15:17: Here, Paul speaks of a boast as if it were an object someone can have. He means that he is rightfully able to boast.
15:18: Here, obedience refers to the Gentiles obeying the command to repent and believe the gospel, which is part of the gospel message.
Here, word and deed could refer to: (1) what Paul had said and done that resulted in the Gentiles trusting in Christ; (2) how the Gentiles displayed their obedience.
Here Paul uses the term word to describe what he had said by using words.
15:19: This clause indicates an additional means by which Christ produced through Paul “the obedience of the Gentiles” that is referred to in the previous verse.
This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word wonders describes the character of the miraculous signs that the Spirit enabled Paul to do.
This clause indicates that the Spirit of God empowered Paul’s “word and deed” and signs and wonders to result in non-Jews trusting in Jesus.
The word Illyricum is the name of a Roman province that was close to Italy.
Paul speaks of preaching the gospel throughout an entire area as if he had fulfilled the gospel.
15:20: The clause not where Christ has been named indicates the kind of places where Paul would not proclaim the gospel.
Here, has been named refers to speaking someone’s name. It does not refer to giving someone a name.
Paul speaks of his work of preaching the gospel and making disciples as if he were building a house on a foundation.
15:21: In this verse Paul quotes Scripture to state that he preaches the gospel to those who have never heard it, which he also stated in the previous verse.
These two clauses mean the same thing. Isaiah says the same thing twice, in slightly different ways, to emphasize that non-Jewish people will hear about the Messiah.
Isaiah implies that the non-Jewish people who never heard about the Messiah will understand who the Messiah is and what he has done.
Paul quotes Isaiah using see to refer to perceiving something.
15:23: μηκέτι τόπον ἔχων ἐν τοῖς κλίμασι τούτοις
Paul uses this clause to imply that there were no more places in his area where people had not heard about Christ.
15:24: At that time, Spain was a Roman province west of Rome.
Paul implies that he would be passing through Rome on his way to Spain.
Here, sent ahead refers to receiving supplies needed for a journey. This is a polite way of asking for food or money.
15:26: Paul uses Macedonia and Achaia here to refer to the Christians who lived in those areas.
15:28: Paul speaks of the money he is taking to Jerusalem as if it were fruit, and he speaks of his delivery of the money as if he were sealing it for the poor believers in Jerusalem.
Paul uses you here to refer to the place where those people lived, which is Rome.
15:29: This could mean: (1) Paul and the believers in Rome will experience Christ’s blessing; (2) Paul will bring Christ’s blessing to the believers in Rome.
Here Paul speaks of abundantly experiencing the blessing of Christ as if it were something that a person could receive in a full amount.
15:30: The two occurrences of by in this verse indicate that what follows each one are the bases for Paul to urge his readers.
Paul speaks of praying fervently as if it were a struggle.
15:31: Here, the disobedient ones refers to the Jews in Judea who disobeyed God by refusing to believe in Jesus.
Here, my service refers to the money that Paul was going to bring to the poor believers in Jerusalem from the believers in Macedonia and Achaia. This is a polite way of referring to bringing money.
Here, for Jerusalem means “for the poor of the saints in Jerusalem,” as mentioned in 15:26.
16:1: Paul speaks of Phoebe as if she were the physical sister of him and his Christian readers. He means she has a brother-sister relationship with all Christians because she trusts in Jesus.
The word Cenchrea was the name of a city in Greece. See how Cenchrea is translated in Acts 18:18.
16:2: Here, in the Lord refers to Phoebe being a fellow believer in the Lord Jesus.
Here, stand by refers to helping someone.
16:3: The word Prisca is the name of a woman who is also called “Priscilla” in Acts 18:2. Aquila is the name of her husband.
Here, fellow workers refers to people who work together with Paul to tell other people about Jesus.
Here, in Christ Jesus could refer to: (1) the kind of work that Prisca and Aquila did with Paul; (2) being united with Christ, as this phrase is used in 3:24; 6:11, 23; 8:1–2, 39; and 15:17.
16:4: This phrase refers to doing something that would put someone in danger of being executed. Romans often executed people by chopping their heads off at the neck with an axe.
Here Paul speaks of expressing thanks as if they were something that he could give to someone.
16:5: The word Epaenetus is the name of a man.
Paul speaks of Epaenetus as if he were fruit that he had harvested. He means that Epaenetus was the first person in Asia who believed in Christ as a result of Paul’s preaching.
16:6: The word Mary is the name of a woman. Several women in the Bible are named Mary because it was a common Jewish name.
16:7: The word Andronicus is the name of a man.

Junias could refer to: (1) a woman named Junia, in which case Andronicus and Junias might be a married couple like Prisca and Aquila. (2) the shortened form of Junianus, a man’s name, which is less likely.
Here, kinsmen could refer to: (1) Jewish Christians; (2) Christian relatives of Paul.
Here, in Christ refers to being united with Christ.
16:8: The word Ampliatus is the name of a man.
16:9: The words Urbanus and Stachys are names of men.
16:10: The words Apelles and Aristobulus are names of men.
16:11: The words Herodion and Narcissus are names of men.
Here, in the Lord refers to being united to Christ and has the same meaning as “in Christ” in 16:7 and 3:24.
16:12: The words Tryphaena, Tryphosa, and Persis are names of women.
16:13: The word Rufus is the name of a man. See how this name is translated in Mark 15:21.
Paul speaks of the mother of Rufus as if she were his own mother. He means that she treated him as if he were her own child.
16:14: Here, with them implies that these people meet together as a church.
16:15: The words Philologus, Nereus, and Olympas are names of men.
The word Julia is the name of a woman. She was probably the wife of Philologus.
16:16: Here, a holy kiss describes a kiss that believers would give to other believers (that is why it is holy). In Paul’s culture, this was an appropriate way to greet someone with whom one was very close, such as a family member or a good friend.
ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ ἐκκλησίαι πᾶσαι τοῦ Χριστοῦ
All here could refer to: (1) all the churches that were in the area where Paul was working when he wrote this letter; (2) all the churches that Paul had authority over or represented.
16:17: τοὺς τὰς διχοστασίας καὶ τὰ σκάνδαλα … ποιοῦντας
This phrase refers to causing believers to argue with each other.
παρὰ τὴν διδαχὴν ἣν ὑμεῖς ἐμάθετε
This clause could refer to: (1) the traps; (2) the means by which these people are causing divisions and traps.
Here, turn away refers to avoiding someone.
16:18: τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν Χριστῷ οὐ δουλεύουσιν
Here, enslaved to our Lord Christ refers to living under the control of our Lord Christ.
Here, stomach could refer to: (1) physical desires, especially the desires to eat or drink; (2) pleasing oneself.
16:19: ἡ … ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴ, εἰς πάντας ἀφίκετο
Here Paul speaks of the Roman believers’ obedience as if it were a person who could go to people. He means that many people had heard about their obedience.
Here, everyone is an exaggeration that Paul uses to show that many believers had heard about the obedience of the Roman believers.
16:20: συντρίψει τὸν Σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑμῶν
Here Paul speaks of the Roman believers having victory over Satan as if they would crush him under their feet.
Paul is using the term with haste to refer something happening without delay. The phrase translated as with haste can also refer to something happening after a very short time period.
As was customary in his culture, Paul closes his letter with a blessing for the Roman believers.
16:21: The words Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater are names of men.
16:22: ἐγὼ, Τέρτιος, ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολὴν

This clause means that Tertius wrote down the words that Paul told him to write in this letter. In ancient times it was common for people to use scribes to physically write dictated letters for them. See the discussion of this in the introduction for this chapter.
16:23: The words Gaius, Erastus, and Quartus are names of men.
ὁ ξένος μου, καὶ ὅλης τῆς ἐκκλησίας
This phrase indicates that the home of Gaius was where Paul and his fellow believers gathered to worship.
Here, steward refers to the person who takes care of the money for the city in which Paul is staying.
16:24: This verse is not in the best earliest manuscripts. It seems to be an accidental repetition of the last part of 16:20.
16:25: Here Paul speaks of God strengthening a person’s faith as if God were establishing that person.
Here, according to indicates that what follows is what Paul’s preaching is based on.

Paul uses the word mystery to refer to God’s plan to save people, which was revealed in the gospel. This does not mean that the idea is hard to understand, but rather, that God had not yet revealed it to people.
